title: Beyond the 956: Juan Atkins, founding father of Detroit techno, dies at 64
excerpt: Juan Atkins, a founding father of Detroit techno and a member of the Belleville Three, has died at 64. His agency announced his death November 1 after he was found unresponsive in his Mexico City hotel room before a planned performance; no official cause of death has been reported.
content:
🌎 BEYOND THE 956

Juan Atkins, the Detroit producer widely known as a founding father of techno, has died at 64.

His death was announced Sunday, November 1, 2026, by Greensmith Artists, the agency that represented him. Speaking to Resident Advisor, a Greensmith representative confirmed that Atkins was found unresponsive in his hotel room in Mexico City before a planned performance at YuYu Cine Club, and was later pronounced dead after being taken to a hospital. The Detroit Free Press reported that he died Saturday, October 31, while in Mexico for a DJ engagement. No official cause of death has been reported.

Born in Detroit in 1962, Atkins grew up in the nearby town of Belleville, where he met future collaborators Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. Together, the three became known as the Belleville Three, whose pioneering work in the early 1980s helped establish Detroit as one of electronic music's most important creative centers.

Atkins's career began in earnest in 1980, when he formed Cybotron with Richard Davis. The duo's 1981 single "Alleys of Your Mind" was an early landmark, and 1983's "Clear" became one of the defining records of the emerging Detroit sound.

After leaving Cybotron, Atkins began releasing music as Model 500. His 1985 track "No UFOs" became a foundational Detroit techno release, and that same year he launched Metroplex, a label that became an important outlet for his own productions and the wider Detroit underground.

Atkins also gave the genre its name. His track "Techno Music" appeared on the seminal 1988 compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit, the release that introduced the Motor City sound to European audiences and fixed the genre's name.

He continued to evolve creatively over the following decades, revisiting Cybotron and developing new material as Model 500 and Infiniti, and collaborating with Moritz von Oswald as Borderland. His productions helped inform a new generation of producers and DJs, and the futuristic, machine-driven aesthetic he helped shape remains at the heart of techno today.

Sources: Resident Advisor; Detroit Free Press; Clash Magazine.
